title: Persistent Prayer, Humble Faith, and the Cost of Following
summary: Jesus tells a parable of a widow who wears down an unjust judge, to teach persistence in prayer, and a parable of a Pharisee and a tax collector at prayer, in which the humble sinner goes home justified. He welcomes little children, tells a wealthy ruler to sell everything and follow him, and for the third time predicts his death and resurrection. Near Jericho he gives sight to a blind beggar who calls him Son of David.
story: The chapter continues directly from the warning about the day of the Son of Man at the end of chapter 17. If that day may be long delayed, disciples need to keep praying and not lose heart, and Jesus asks whether he will find faith on earth when he comes. The rest of the chapter answers the question of who enters the kingdom. Not the self-assured Pharisee but the tax collector who begs for mercy. Not the rich ruler who keeps the commandments but cannot let go of his wealth, but those who receive the kingdom like a child. Luke has been following his own path through Jesus' teaching since 9:51; here he rejoins the order of Mark, and Jesus draws near Jericho, the last stop before Jerusalem.
historical:
The temple in Jerusalem, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great from about 20 BC, was the center of Jewish worship. Public prayer was offered there at the times of the morning and afternoon sacrifices (Acts 3:1 mentions the hour of prayer in the afternoon), and people came up to pray on their own as well. Tax collectors in Judea and Galilee were local men who collected tolls and taxes on behalf of Roman authorities or Herodian rulers, often by contracting for the right and keeping what they could take above the required amount. They were widely despised as collaborators and cheats.

Jericho lay about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem, near the Jordan, and was the usual starting point for the steep climb up to the city for pilgrims coming from Galilee by the Jordan valley. Herod the Great had built a winter palace there, and New Testament Jericho sat near the older ruined city. Mark places the healing of blind Bartimaeus as Jesus was leaving Jericho, while Luke has him approaching it; interpreters have suggested that the old and new sites of Jericho lying side by side, or simple differences in how each writer arranged the story, account for the difference.
cultural:
Widows in the ancient world were among the most vulnerable people, often without a male protector to argue their case, and the Law repeatedly commands justice for the widow and the orphan. A judge who neither fears God nor respects people fails both duties at once. The widow's only weapon is persistence, and the judge's phrase about her wearing him out is, literally, that she might give him a black eye, a colorful idiom for wearing him down.

The Pharisee's practices went beyond what the Law required. The Law commanded only one annual fast, on the Day of Atonement, but some devout Jews fasted twice a week, and the early Christian manual called the Didache, noting that others fasted on Mondays and Thursdays, tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays instead. He also tithed everything he acquired, not only what the Law specified. Standing apart and beating one's breast was a sign of deep grief. In the camel saying, the camel was the largest animal in Palestine and the needle's eye the smallest opening, a deliberate picture of impossibility. The popular idea that a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye lies behind the saying has no ancient support.
literary: Luke frames both opening parables by telling the reader their point in advance (verses 1 and 9), an unusual feature. The two parables form a pair on prayer: one on persistence, one on humility. The first argues from the lesser to the greater: if even an unjust judge gives in to persistence, how much more will God, who is just and loves his elect. The second uses sharp contrast and reversal, summed up in a saying Luke has used before (14:11): “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” The scenes that follow pair two more figures: children who bring nothing and a ruler who has everything. The ruler's question echoes the lawyer's question in 10:25, and the chapter closes with a blind man who sees who Jesus is while the disciples, in verse 34, do not understand.

outline.t: The widow and the unjust judge
The Pharisee and the tax collector
Receiving the kingdom like a child
The rich ruler and the cost of the kingdom
Jesus predicts his death and resurrection a third time
A blind beggar near Jericho receives his sight

doctrines.note: Jesus teaches that his people ought always to pray and not lose heart, because God is not like the unjust judge: he hears his elect who cry to him day and night. The second parable adds that God hears the prayer that pleads for mercy, not the one that reports its own merits.

The tax collector goes home justified, declared right with God, without having done anything but confess his sin and ask for mercy. When the disciples ask who then can be saved, Jesus answers that what is impossible with man is possible with God. Salvation is God's work, received like a child receives.

Jesus asks whether the Son of Man will find faith on earth. The chapter's answer is shown in people: the persistent widow, the tax collector, the children, and the blind man who calls out all the louder and hears, “Your faith has healed you.”

words.note: Hilaskomai, to be propitiated or to show mercy. The tax collector's prayer is literally, God, be propitiated toward me, the sinner. The word belongs to the language of sacrifice and atonement; scholars debate whether its emphasis falls on wrath turned aside or on sin covered and removed, and many see both. Standing in the temple where sacrifices were offered, he asks God to deal with his sin as only God can.

Dikaioō, to justify, to declare righteous. It is a legal term for a verdict, not a description of moral improvement. Jesus says the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified. Paul later builds his teaching on justification by faith with the same word, and this parable shows its roots in Jesus' own teaching.

Ekdikēsis, justice or vindication, from the same root as the widow's plea, give me justice. The word can mean punishment of wrongdoers, but here it means God's righting of wrongs for those who have been wronged. The parable promises that God will vindicate his people.

christ: The blind man twice calls Jesus Son of David, the royal title of the Messiah promised to David's line, and Jesus does not silence him. Jesus is about to enter Jerusalem as king. Yet in verses 31 to 33 he describes what that kingship will cost: he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, and killed, and on the third day he will rise. He says that everything the prophets wrote about the Son of Man will be fulfilled, a theme Luke brings to its climax in chapter 24. The rich ruler calls him good teacher, and Jesus' reply, that no one is good except God alone, is not a denial of his own goodness but an invitation to think about what that title implies about the one who bears it.

hard.q: Must every follower of Jesus sell everything, as the rich ruler was told?
hard.a: Jesus' command to the ruler is direct and total, and it should not be softened into a suggestion. Yet Luke does not present it as a rule for every disciple: in the next chapter Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor and Jesus declares that salvation has come to his house, and Luke mentions women who supported Jesus from their own means (8:3). Many interpreters conclude that Jesus diagnosed the particular thing that held this man, his wealth, and demanded its surrender because it stood between him and following. Others, including many monastic traditions across church history, have taken the command as a real call to voluntary poverty for some. What no reading can escape is the principle: whatever a person will not give up for Jesus has become a rival to him, and wealth is named as an especially powerful rival. Jesus also promises that no one who leaves home or family for the kingdom will fail to receive far more.

questions: Jesus told the parable of the widow so that his disciples would not lose heart. What prayer have you been tempted to stop praying?
The Pharisee compared himself with the tax collector. Whom do you compare yourself with, and what does that comparison hide from you?
What would it mean for you to receive the kingdom of God like a little child, bringing nothing to earn it?
